title: FinOps Framework 2026 adds strategy alignment and broader technology guidance
description: A background brief on the March framework revision and its relevance to resource-management objectives.
text:
What changed
The FinOps Foundation’s [19 March 2026 framework update]() introduced Executive Strategy Alignment as a capability and expanded guidance around scopes and technology categories. The announcement includes AI among the technology categories addressed.

This brief covers that published revision as background, rather than presenting the March announcement as new today.

 Why it matters
Editorial interpretation: an automated allocation policy needs an explicit business objective. Minimizing immediate spending, reducing waiting, and preserving capacity for experimentation can lead to different decisions. A cost controller needs to know which tradeoff its owner has authorized.

Read [FinOps and cost controls](/wiki/finops-and-cost-controls/) for the distinction between forecasts, alerts, resource quotas, and enforced spending limits. [Human oversight](/wiki/human-oversight/) explains why a budget boundary also needs an accountable owner.

 Limits of the evidence
This is the framework publisher’s description of its own update. It does not establish adoption rates, measured savings, or the effectiveness of any automated product. The implications for resource-control design above are editorial interpretation, not a benchmark result or a requirement imposed by the Foundation.

title: Kubernetes 1.36 expands Dynamic Resource Allocation
description: A background brief on the DRA team’s May 2026 update, with adoption questions for resource operators.
text:
What changed
In its [7 May 2026 update](), the Kubernetes DRA team described changes to Dynamic Resource Allocation in version 1.36, including feature graduations, additional capabilities, and a broader driver ecosystem. The announcement discusses specialized hardware as well as work involving CPU and memory resources.

This is background coverage of that announcement, not a claim that version 1.36 is the latest Kubernetes release.

 Why it matters
Editorial interpretation: resource operators should evaluate the exact allocation capability their workloads need, rather than treating “DRA support” as a single feature. Hardware requirements, drivers, and the maturity of individual capabilities affect what a deployment can use.

A useful evaluation question is whether an allocation request expresses the actual constraints of the workload. See [resource scheduling](/wiki/resource-scheduling/) for the distinction between eligible capacity and preferred capacity.

 Limits of the evidence
The source is a project announcement. This brief does not independently test the features, establish compatibility with a specific cluster, or substantiate performance gains. Check the documentation and feature state for the exact version and driver being evaluated.

The announcement is evidence of reported project changes, not evidence that every resource-management deployment should adopt them.

title: Headlamp guide separates Kueue admission from Pod scheduling
description: An October 2026 project guide illustrates why a queued workload may wait before Pod placement begins.
text:
What changed
A [14 October 2026 Kubernetes project guide]() describes investigating Kueue admission through Headlamp. It distinguishes the decision to admit a workload under queue policy and quota from the later placement of Pods on nodes.

The guide uses the Kueue plugin’s 0.1.0-alpha release. It describes read-only Kueue views, while noting that Headlamp’s standard resource actions remain subject to the user’s permissions.

 Why it matters
Editorial interpretation: diagnosing a resource delay starts with locating the decision that is waiting. A workload that has not been admitted needs a different investigation from one whose Pods cannot find eligible nodes.

This distinction can prevent an operator from treating every pending job as a shortage of physical capacity. See [resource scheduling](/wiki/resource-scheduling/) and [observability](/wiki/observability/) for related concepts.

 Limits of the evidence
This is a summary of a project-authored guide, not an independent evaluation. The plugin is identified as alpha in the source. This brief does not test compatibility, measure troubleshooting speed, or establish that a particular cluster has an admission problem.

Read the original guide for prerequisites and version-specific details before applying its procedure.

title: About this reference
description: Purpose, authorship, editorial boundaries, and how this resource is maintained.
text:
A reference for resource decisions
This site helps readers understand how automated systems allocate resources and how people can inspect and govern those decisions. Its initial focus is compute infrastructure, workload coordination, technology costs, and human oversight.

The project aims to earn trust through useful explanations, primary citations, clear limitations, and visible corrections. It does not claim to be the definitive authority or a standards body.

 Maintainer and authorship
Mason Nguyen maintains the site and its public source repository. “ARM Editorial” identifies this site's editorial voice; it is not a claim that an independent editorial board exists. The initial reference articles were prepared with AI assistance, as disclosed on each article.

The proposed [ARM working framework](/framework/) is attributed separately. Its existence does not establish consensus around that framework or the site's terminology.

 Commercial boundaries
This reference has no service checkout or commercial referral directory. Earlier versions directed readers to implementation businesses. The standalone revision removes those pathways while retaining accountable authorship. Removing referrals should not be read as a claim that the maintainer has no outside commercial interests.

Relevant affiliations must be disclosed when they affect a covered subject. See the [editorial policy](/editorial-policy/) for the conflict-of-interest rule.

 Maintenance and accountability
Readers can propose source additions and corrections through [GitHub](). Changes are versioned, and material editorial changes are summarized in the [revision log](/changelog/).

The wiki is curated rather than open to immediate anonymous publication. Contributions are welcome; publication depends on evidence, relevance, and editorial review.

 Historical work records
The earlier [public-practice records](/practice/) remain available as historical, first-party work records. They are not independent validation of this reference, product recommendations, or evidence of industry consensus.

title: Revision log

text:

title: Contribute or request a correction
description: A practical route for improving definitions, citations, examples, and industry coverage.
text:
Suggest a factual correction
[Open a correction request]() with the page URL, the exact passage, a proposed correction, and a supporting source. State whether the issue is a factual error, outdated information, unclear wording, or a missing perspective.

GitHub requires an account to submit an issue. Please omit private operational data, credentials, and personal information from public reports.

 Contribute an article
Use the [public repository]() to propose a Markdown article or an edit. Explain the topic's relevance, cite original sources, and distinguish sourced facts from your own examples and analysis.

Disclose relevant affiliations. State whether AI assisted with drafting or verification. Do not invent review credentials or imply that a cited project endorses this site.

 Suggest industry coverage
[Suggest a source or story](). Include the original announcement or research, its date, and the resource-management question it affects. A suggestion does not guarantee coverage.

 How changes are reviewed
Submissions are checked for factual support, neutral wording, relevant scope, and clear limitations. Technical checks validate internal links and required article metadata. Passing those checks is not a substitute for editorial judgment.

The maintainer decides whether to publish. Material corrections are recorded in the [revision log](/changelog/), and each article links to its source history.

title: Editorial policy
description: How this reference handles neutrality, sources, uncertainty, AI assistance, and corrections.
text:
Purpose and scope
Autonomous Resource Management is an editorially maintained knowledge resource about automated allocation, orchestration, infrastructure, and oversight. Coverage is selected for its relevance and evidence, not for its ability to refer readers to a commercial provider.

 Neutral point of view
Describe what a source demonstrates and what remains uncertain. Attribute disputed claims. Give approaches attention proportional to their relevance and supporting evidence; neutrality does not require giving unsupported claims equal weight.

Separate established technical concepts, the site's proposed framework, and dated industry developments. Examples and recommendations must be labeled as editorial guidance unless directly supported by cited evidence.

 Source standards
Prefer original specifications, project documentation, public research, and official announcements for factual descriptions. An official announcement establishes what its publisher says; it does not independently validate performance or market leadership.

For claims of effectiveness, seek reproducible evidence and independent evaluation where available. Identify preprints, vendor benchmarks, and conflicts of interest. Cite evidence near the claim and explain each source's scope in the references.

 News and review
News briefs distinguish the date of the source event from this site's publication date. Each brief explains what changed, why it may matter, and the limits of the evidence. Older developments may be covered as background; they must not be presented as breaking news.

Automated discovery places candidates in an editorial queue. It does not publish articles. Before publication, an editor checks the original source, dates, attribution, scope, related wiki entries, and correction needs. The publication record identifies whether the source check was human or AI-assisted. Do not imply independent testing or expert review when neither occurred.

 AI assistance
AI may assist with discovery, drafting, source comparison, and maintenance. Launch articles disclose AI-assisted source synthesis. No invented human reviewer, interview, test result, or credential may be added. A maintainer remains responsible for accepting and correcting published content.

 Ownership and conflicts
The site is maintained by Mason Nguyen. The previous homepage linked to commercial implementation properties; those referral paths have been removed from the reference site's navigation and content model. This change does not establish independent ownership or erase relevant affiliations.

Contributors must disclose a relevant commercial relationship when covering an affiliated product or organization. The site does not sell favorable coverage, rankings, or placement in its reference articles. Author attribution is retained.

 Corrections and revision dates
Report a correction through the [contribution page](/contribute/). Include the URL, disputed passage, and evidence. Material factual corrections receive a visible note and a revision-history entry. Update dates change for substantive edits, not to create an appearance of freshness.

 Reuse and attribution
Summarize sources in original language and link to the original. Do not reproduce full third-party articles or images without permission. Source code visibility does not grant rights to third-party material. This site makes no blanket open-content licensing claim.

title: The ARM working framework
description: An attributed proposal for organizing decision rights, signals, recovery, escalation, and audit evidence.
text:
Status and authorship
This working framework was developed by Mason Nguyen and is maintained here as an editorial proposal. It is not an industry standard, certification scheme, or independently validated assurance model. The reference library covers established concepts separately from this synthesis.

Earlier versions of the homepage placed this framework at the center of the ARM definition. This revision gives it a dedicated location so readers can distinguish the proposal from the broader subject.

 Five design concerns
 Decision rights
Identify the principal who grants authority, the permitted actions, and the limits of delegation. The proposal recommends explicit approval for actions outside the delegated scope.

 Observable signals
Record the measurements and assumptions used in a decision. [OpenTelemetry's signal vocabulary]() is relevant background for instrumentation, not an endorsement of this framework.

 Recoverable state
Define how interrupted work is identified and recovered. Checkpoints and durable records can help, but their guarantees depend on implementation. This framework does not promise recovery from every failure mode or zero data loss.

 Human escalation
Define the conditions that require review and the action taken while review is pending. [NIST's AI risk-management work]() supplies broader context; these five concerns are not NIST's categories.

 Auditable decisions
Connect requests, permission, execution, and observed results. Use precise descriptions of retention and tamper resistance instead of assuming a log is immutable.

 Applying the proposal
For a hypothetical resource controller, write down one permitted action, one limit, its input signal, its recovery behavior, and its escalation owner. Then test a missing signal, a rejected allocation, and an uncertain result.

This exercise is an editorial method for revealing assumptions. It does not establish that a system is safe, optimal, or compliant.

 What would strengthen the framework
Independent critique, reproducible examples, failure reports, and comparisons with alternative designs would make the proposal more useful. Contributions should identify which claim they support or challenge. Use the [contribution guide](/contribute/) to propose a change.

 Related reference material
Start with [autonomous resource management](/wiki/autonomous-resource-management/), [human oversight](/wiki/human-oversight/), and [audit trails](/wiki/audit-trails/). Search visibility and structured publishing are separate concerns; they are not prerequisites for a working resource controller.

title: Agent orchestration and tool access
description: Coordinating work while keeping authority, retries, and external actions explicit.
text:
Coordination and authority
Agent orchestration coordinates tasks, state, tools, and dependencies. Resource management enters when a workflow consumes execution slots, model calls, compute time, or budget.

An orchestration system may use deterministic rules, AI-assisted decisions, or a mixture. A language model's proposed action should be distinguishable from the component authorized to execute it.

 Protocols have a specific scope
The [Model Context Protocol architecture, revision 2025-06-18](), describes hosts, clients, and servers with distinct responsibilities. A connection to a tool server is not evidence that every possible operation is appropriate for a particular user or workflow.

Protocol support should therefore be documented separately from resource limits, permission checks, and evidence of successful execution. This article cites a specific protocol revision; consult the project's current specification when implementing.

 A bounded workflow example
Imagine an agent that proposes resizing a service. A useful separation is:

1. Collect current workload and cost evidence.
2. Produce a proposal with assumptions and an expiry time.
3. Check permitted resources, spending limits, and required approval.
4. Execute the approved action with an operation identifier.
5. Inspect the actual outcome and record failures or partial completion.

This is an editorial design example, not a required protocol workflow.

 Retries and uncertainty
A timeout can mean an action failed, succeeded, or is still running. Repeating a request without checking its status can create duplicate work or spending. Recovery design should specify how to recognize an existing operation and when to ask for human intervention.

Related reading: [human oversight](/wiki/human-oversight/), [audit trails](/wiki/audit-trails/), and the proposed [ARM working framework](/framework/).

title: Audit trails and decision provenance
description: Recording what was requested, authorized, executed, and observed.
text:
What an audit trail can establish
An audit trail records events so that a decision or action can be examined later. In a resource system, useful events include a request, its authorization context, the attempted action, and the result.

[Kubernetes auditing]() provides a concrete example of configurable records for API activity. What is recorded depends on the audit policy and backend configuration.

 Design around questions
An editorial starting point is to ask whether a reviewer can determine:

1. Who or what requested the change?
2. Which policy or approval permitted it?
3. Which measurements were available at the time?
4. Was the action attempted, completed, rejected, or left uncertain?
5. What subsequent evidence confirms the outcome?

Use identifiers to connect related events. Keep the original event time distinct from the time a record was received or reviewed.

 Integrity and privacy
“Immutable” is a strong claim. Retention rules, access restrictions, integrity checks, and independent copies provide different protections. State the protections actually implemented rather than assuming that a logging product makes records tamper-proof.

Logs can also contain sensitive information. Decide what is necessary to retain, who can access it, and how long it remains useful. An exhaustive transcript is not automatically the best audit record.

 Limits
A record of an authorized request does not prove the action succeeded. A record of success does not by itself prove that the action was appropriate. Missing records can reflect a collection failure rather than the absence of activity.

Combine audit evidence with [observability](/wiki/observability/) and [human review](/wiki/human-oversight/). Claims about system reliability need tests and operational evidence beyond the existence of logs.

title: What is autonomous resource management?
description: A practical introduction to resource decisions, feedback loops, operating limits, and human accountability.
text:
Definition and scope
Autonomous resource management describes systems that observe resource conditions and adjust allocations within defined operating limits. In this reference, resources include compute capacity, storage, workload slots, and technology budgets. This is the site's working scope, not a claim that one definition is universally standardized.

A useful example is a service that adds capacity when demand rises, subject to an upper limit and a response-time objective. The word “autonomous” describes the delegated decision scope; it does not establish that the system uses an AI model or can safely operate without supervision.

 How the pieces fit together
A resource-management design needs a target, measurements, a decision mechanism, and a way to act. Kubernetes documents a concrete form of this pattern: [controllers reconcile observed state with desired state](). The broader connection to ARM is our editorial synthesis.

Consider a queue of image-processing jobs. A controller may observe queue age, request more workers, and stop increasing capacity at a configured limit. A complete operational design must also decide what happens when metrics disappear, capacity is unavailable, or the next action exceeds the approved budget. Those are design questions, not benefits automatically conferred by automation.

 Related disciplines
- [Autoscaling](/wiki/autoscaling/) changes capacity in response to signals.
- [Resource scheduling](/wiki/resource-scheduling/) decides where work can run.
- [Orchestration](/wiki/agent-orchestration/) coordinates dependent work and tool interactions.
- [FinOps and cost controls](/wiki/finops-and-cost-controls/) connect resource use to financial accountability. The [FinOps Framework]() describes an operating practice that involves engineering, finance, and business participants.
- [Human oversight](/wiki/human-oversight/) addresses authority, review, and intervention.

 Boundaries and open questions
The appropriate degree of autonomy depends on the reversibility of an action, the reliability of its evidence, and the people affected. A low-risk scaling decision and an irreversible spending commitment should not be treated as equivalent.

The [ARM working framework](/framework/) offers one proposed way to organize these questions. Its five design concerns are an attributed synthesis rather than an industry standard or a prerequisite for every automated resource system.

title: Autoscaling and feedback loops
description: How capacity follows demand, and why signals, limits, and recovery matter.
text:
What autoscaling changes
Autoscaling adjusts capacity in response to observed or anticipated demand. The [Kubernetes documentation distinguishes horizontal scaling, vertical scaling, and infrastructure scaling](). Adding replicas, changing resources assigned to a workload, and adding nodes affect different parts of a system.

Choosing a scaling mechanism starts with the bottleneck. More application replicas may not help a saturated shared database. More node capacity may not help an application that cannot use it.

 Signals and decisions
A controller compares measurements with a target and requests a change. Signals might include queue age, request latency, or resource utilization. The useful signal depends on what the service is trying to achieve.

For a hypothetical batch queue, an editor's design example is: add one worker when the oldest job exceeds an agreed wait threshold, cap the worker count, and require a stable period before removing capacity. The example illustrates decision structure; it is not a tested production configuration.

 Tradeoffs to evaluate
- Responsiveness: a fast reaction can reduce waiting but may chase short-lived noise.
- Stability: frequent opposing adjustments can interrupt work or waste capacity.
- Cost: spare capacity can improve response time while increasing spend.
- Availability: a request to scale does not prove that capacity was obtained.

Review these tradeoffs together. [Cost controls](/wiki/finops-and-cost-controls/) and [observability](/wiki/observability/) make the operating consequences easier to inspect.

 Failure and recovery
Specify the response to stale metrics, failed allocations, quota exhaustion, and interrupted scale-down. Test those responses against the actual workload. A controller should not interpret missing demand data as proof that demand is zero.

The underlying loop is described in [Kubernetes controller concepts](). Applying that pattern to a particular service still requires workload-specific measurement and testing.

title: FinOps and cost controls
description: Relating resource consumption, budgets, and business outcomes without assuming automatic savings.
text:
Financial accountability
The [FinOps Framework]() brings technology usage and value into a collaborative operating practice. Resource automation can support that practice, but a technical controller does not replace decisions about ownership and business priorities.

A useful distinction is between a spending forecast, an alert, and an enforced limit. A forecast estimates a future outcome. An alert informs someone. An enforced limit constrains an action. Treating them as interchangeable can leave an automated workflow with more spending authority than intended.

 Design the budget boundary
For a hypothetical inference service, identify who owns the budget, which usage is counted, when usage data becomes available, and what happens at a limit. Decide whether the service queues work, degrades gracefully, requests approval, or stops accepting new tasks.

A cost cap also has operational consequences. Stopping a critical service to avoid overspending may be an unacceptable policy; that tradeoff needs an accountable decision before the incident.

 Resource limits are not currency limits
[Kubernetes resource quotas]() can constrain resource requests or object counts. Their units and scope differ from a bill denominated in currency. Translating a resource allowance into a cost expectation requires pricing assumptions and usage context.

 Evaluate claims carefully
When someone reports savings, ask which baseline, workload, period, prices, and service-quality targets were used. Distinguish a projected saving from an observed reduction in paid costs. A lower cost per operation can coexist with higher total spend if demand grows.

These evaluation questions are editorial guidance. This site does not claim that any particular allocation policy guarantees a financial outcome.

Related: [autoscaling](/wiki/autoscaling/), [resource scheduling](/wiki/resource-scheduling/), and [observability](/wiki/observability/).

title: Human oversight and decision rights
description: Defining who can authorize, interrupt, and review automated resource decisions.
text:
Oversight needs an operational meaning
Human oversight is useful when it identifies a person or role, a decision they can make, and a practical way to intervene. A dashboard alone does not establish that somebody can stop an action or restore an acceptable state.

The [NIST AI Risk Management Framework]() provides voluntary guidance for managing AI risks. Applying it to a resource-management system requires context; citing it does not demonstrate compliance or certification.

 Define the delegated scope
As an editorial design checklist, document:

- Which resources and actions the system may control.
- The limits on amount, duration, and frequency.
- Which actions need approval before execution.
- Who can pause the system and revoke access.
- How an operator learns about a failed or incomplete action.

Separate permission from confidence. A system can be highly confident about an action it is not authorized to take.

 Escalation example
A hypothetical workflow may automatically add a small amount of reversible capacity, require approval for a larger change, and refuse to make an irreversible commitment without explicit authorization. If the approver is unavailable, the policy must specify whether to wait, retain the existing state, or follow another documented fallback.

Silence should not be interpreted as newly granted authority. This is the site's design recommendation, not a quoted NIST requirement.

 Review and learning
After a consequential event, compare the authorized action, the recorded action, and the observed outcome. Update the policy when evidence shows that an assumption was wrong. Document unresolved questions as well as successes.

Related: [agent orchestration](/wiki/agent-orchestration/), [audit trails](/wiki/audit-trails/), and [the proposed ARM framework](/framework/).

title: Observability for resource decisions
description: Connecting measurements to actions without mistaking telemetry for proof of correctness.
text:
Observe the system and its decisions
Observability helps operators investigate system behavior from available evidence. [OpenTelemetry describes signals such as traces, metrics, and logs](), which offer different views of system activity.

For resource management, an operational question is not only “what was the CPU load?” but “which measurement led to this allocation, and what happened afterward?” Connecting the decision to its inputs makes that question easier to investigate.

 A useful decision record
As editorial guidance, consider recording the resource identifier, observation time, policy version, requested change, and resulting state. Record units and measurement windows too: a point-in-time value and a ten-minute average can support different conclusions.

Separate an action request from its acknowledgement and eventual outcome. A successful API response is not necessarily evidence that a service met its objective.

 Evidence quality
A signal can be delayed, sampled, missing, or incorrectly labeled. Before using a metric to control resources, define how old it may be and how the system should behave when the data is unavailable.

For example, a hypothetical capacity controller could hold its last safe allocation and notify an operator when its demand signal becomes stale. That is one possible policy, not a universal default.

 Limits
Telemetry does not independently prove causation, security, compliance, or optimal allocation. A before-and-after cost chart can be affected by workload changes and pricing changes. Claims about an improvement should identify those conditions and the comparison baseline.

Use [audit trails](/wiki/audit-trails/) to preserve decision context and [human oversight](/wiki/human-oversight/) to define who responds when evidence is insufficient.

title: Resource scheduling and allocation
description: Placement decisions, competing objectives, and the difference between capacity and usable capacity.
text:
What a scheduler decides
A scheduler matches work to eligible resources. It has to respect constraints before considering preferences. [Kubernetes describes filtering candidate nodes and scoring the feasible ones]().

Scheduling is distinct from scaling. A placement decision can rearrange work within existing capacity; a scaling decision changes available capacity. They interact, but neither alone guarantees that a workload meets its objective.

 Constraints before preferences
In a hypothetical accelerator queue, eligibility might depend on memory, device compatibility, and data location. Preferences might favor shorter completion time or lower estimated cost. An inexpensive resource that cannot run the task is not a valid choice.

Record which constraints are mandatory and which objectives can be traded off. A single “efficiency” score can conceal conflicts between throughput, fairness, latency, and expense.

 Questions for an allocation policy
1. Which workloads can wait, and for how long?
2. Can lower-priority work be interrupted without losing progress?
3. How is scarce capacity shared between teams?
4. What happens when no eligible resource exists?
5. What evidence explains a rejected or delayed allocation?

These questions are editorial design guidance. Answers need to be validated against the workload and the resource provider.

 Limits and related concepts
[Resource quotas]() constrain resource consumption within Kubernetes namespaces. A quota should not be confused with a financial budget or a guarantee of physical availability.

Read [autoscaling](/wiki/autoscaling/) for capacity adjustments and [audit trails](/wiki/audit-trails/) for recording decisions. Evaluate allocation policies using declared workload conditions rather than unqualified utilization or savings claims.
